outcome: Since 26 January 2024 no event settles the conjecture for all n or for any further n. The large-n theorem (Kang, Kelly, Kühn, Methuku, Osthus; arXiv January 2021, Annals of Mathematics 2023) predates the window and leaves an unstated finite range of small n open. Post-window events are a conditional bound on the stronger Berge–Füredi conjecture (2024, 2025), an expository article (2025), a site status discussion (2025), and a Lean statement file (2026) whose key variants use sorry.
problem_asks: Part 1 (the whole content): for every positive integer n, not only large n, given any family of n complete graphs (cliques) each with exactly n vertices, such that any two of them share at most one vertex, the union graph G has chromatic number at most n, so chi(G) = n (the lower bound chi(G) >= n is immediate from one K_n). Wikipedia words it with k in place of n. Equivalent forms the statement supplies: (a) hypergraph form: every simple (linear) hypergraph on n vertices has chromatic index at most n; (b) set-system form: given n sets of size n pairwise meeting in at most one element, the union of the sets can be coloured with n colours so that every set contains all n colours. The statement asks for nothing about cliques of order k different from n, nor about the Erdős–Füredi variant with pairwise intersections of size at most k, nor about any bound other than the exact value n.

events.what_happened: Sang-Un Lee (Gangneung-Wonju National University) published in the Journal of the Korean Internet Broadcasting and Communication Society, vol. 15 no. 1, pp. 269–276 (February 2015), a paper titled in English ‘Proof Algorithm of Erdös-Faber-Lovász Conjecture’. Its abstract says it ‘proves the Erdös-Faber-Lovász conjecture … which is so far unresolved’. The only supporting evidence the abstract describes is an algorithm tested on K_k-clique-sum intersecting graphs with 3 ≤ k ≤ 8, where it obtained chromatic number k in every case.
events.delivers: Claims the full conjecture for all k. The abstract's evidence covers only 3 ≤ k ≤ 8 on a stated class (K_k-clique-sum intersecting graphs); the abstract describes no general argument. I did not read the body.
events.remains: Everything beyond the claim, by the abstract's own account: the general step is not shown there.
events.time_since_posted: about 11 years; no review, citation or acceptance found in the sources I could reach
events.doubts: The general claim rests on the small-k computations the abstract describes. No independent check, citing paper or acceptance found. It was published in a venue outside the main combinatorics literature, and I did not read the body.
events.direction: Asserts the conjecture (chromatic number equals k for the union) for all k; the evidence in the abstract covers only 3 ≤ k ≤ 8.

events.what_happened: S. M. Hegde and Suresh Dara, ‘On Erdős–Faber–Lovász Conjecture’, arXiv:1701.04550, v1 only, submitted 17 January 2017. The abstract proves two special cases: if each clique has at most √n vertices of clique degree greater than 1, the union is n-colourable; and if each clique has at most ⌈(n+d−1)/d⌉ vertices of clique degree at least d, the union is n-colourable. The journal page does not mention the arXiv number, so the link between the two is inferred from title and abstract.

Theorem 1.1 in the HTML version reads: ‘For every sufficiently large n, every linear hypergraph H on n vertices has chromatic index at most n.’ The paper also gives stability versions that confirm a prediction of Kahn, and states that the proof can be turned into a randomised polynomial-time algorithm (Introduction, citing their reference [34]). v2 9 July 2021; v3 25 January 2023, ‘Final version, to appear in the Annals of Mathematics’. Published Annals of Mathematics 198(2) (2023), pp. 537–618, DOI 10.4007/annals.2023.198.2.2; received 12 January 2021, accepted 19 January 2023, online 31 August 2023. The algorithmic companion appeared at FOCS 2021 (pp. 1080–1089; publication dated 4 March 2022 on the Birmingham portal).

Small n are covered only by the older finite verifications (Hindman 1981; Romero and Alonso-Pecina 2014, if correct). Between those ranges and n₀ I found no source that covers the gap.

events.what_happened: Kang, Kelly, Kühn, Methuku and Osthus, ‘Solution to a problem of Erdős on the chromatic index of hypergraphs with bounded codegree’, arXiv:2110.06181 (v1 12 October 2021; v2 19 October 2024, ‘Final version, to appear in Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society’). It answers Erdős’s 1977 question for t ≥ 2: the largest chromatic number of a union of complete graphs on at most n vertices that pairwise share at most t vertices, dually the largest chromatic index of an n-vertex hypergraph with maximum degree ≤ (1−o(1))tn and maximum codegree ≤ t. Theorem 1.2 covers t ≥ 2 with n ≥ n₀ (n₀ an absolute constant). Its t = 1 content (Theorem 1.3) assumes Δ(H) ≤ (1−ε)n and gives a list-colouring version. The paper cites the EFL case t = 1 as already proved for all sufficiently large n (its reference [18]).
events.revisions: v2 19 Oct 2024 (PLMS final version, to appear)
events.delivers: For t ≥ 2, a different question from EFL (which is t = 1): the bound tn, with equality for t-fold projective planes. For t = 1 it gives only Theorem 1.3, which needs the extra assumption Δ(H) ≤ (1−ε)n. That is a restricted version of EFL, not the general case.
events.remains: The t = 1 conjecture without the degree assumption, which is the problem as stated. The paper does not claim a new proof of it.

events.what_happened: Dhruv Mubayi and Jacques Verstraete, ‘Coloring hypergraphs that are the union of nearly disjoint cliques’, arXiv:2304.04855 (submitted 10 April 2023, v1 only). Studies the maximum chromatic number of hypergraphs formed from cliques with small pairwise intersections. It builds near designs with polynomially many cliques and shows they have large chromatic number, gives lower bounds for the case of pairwise intersections at most one via a random greedy process, and gives bounds on caps in projective and affine planes. The abstract does not mention the Erdős–Faber–Lovász conjecture.

The abstract gives upper bounds on the chromatic index q(V,E) of linear loopless hypergraphs, via a colour-preserving group acting on proper minimally edge-coloured linear hypergraphs. It presents this as ‘a plausible approach to solving the Berge–Füredi conjecture’, with a bound relating q to Δ([H]₂)+1, and gives three sufficient conditions, involving the Helly property, under which Berge–Füredi holds within the framework. The abstract does not mention EFL.

events.what_happened: On the erdosproblems.com forum thread attached to Problem #19, participants discuss the status of the EFL case. TerenceTao (1 September 2025 in the fetched summary) reads the commentary as saying the problem is not fully resolved but reduced to a decidable finite check. zach_hunter (3 September 2025) argues it should be green (more solved than open) rather than red. Tao replies (4 September) that the site keeps a binary official status and uses the community database for the ‘decidable’ label. Thomas Bloom (7 September) agrees it is more on the solved side than open, while noting remaining work and a bias to treating ‘for all large enough integers’ as good enough. The thread title reads ‘DECIDABLE Resolved up to a finite check. - $500’. A post by ‘dykang’ (dated 25 November 2025 in the fetched summary) says Theorem 1.2 of arXiv:2110.06181 proves the Erdős–Füredi generalisation (pairwise intersections at most k, with k ≠ n) for n ≥ n₀, and that with Horák–Tuza only finitely many (k,n) with k < √n and n < n₀ remain. Other posts (Alfaiz, 2 December 2025; Bloom, 6 December 2025) concern references. The fetched summary lists these dates out of chronological order, so the ordering is unverified.

disputes.summary: The Erdős Problems site labels the problem ‘DECIDABLE – Resolved up to a finite check’ (forum thread title) and declines a binary solved label (Tao, Sept 2025). Forum participants disagree on whether it counts as solved. The Formal Conjectures repository labels its large-n and n < 10 variants ‘research solved’ with sorry-based proofs. Wikipedia’s lead says the conjecture ‘for all sufficiently large values of k was proved’.
Hindman (1981) small-n range: erdosproblems says n < 10; Wikipedia says all simple hypergraphs with L ≤ 10, i.e. n ≤ 10. The primary paper was not opened.

Small-n verification claims conflict in range: Hindman (n ≤ 10 or n < 10), Romero and Alonso-Pecina (n ≤ 12, 2014 record only), and Kirchweger–Peitl–Szeider (extension to ‘larger values’, range not stated). The threshold n₀ of the large-n theorem is unstated, so the residue cannot be fixed from the sources.

Two 2015 claims of a complete proof for all n (Lee, Korean journal, abstract evidence only for 3 ≤ k ≤ 8; Hegde and Dara, arXiv:1508.03476) have no acceptance or citation I found. The 2021 KKKMO proof, accepted in the Annals in 2023, is the one that the Erdős site, Wikipedia and the Formal Conjectures repository credit. I found no author-level priority dispute.
The Erdős–Füredi (k ≠ n) forum argument, based on Theorem 1.2 of arXiv:2110.06181, is a claim about a different question. The thread does not treat it as settling EFL.

summary: Problem #19 on erdosproblems.com is the Erdős–Faber–Lovász conjecture, and the main result is Kang, Kelly, Kühn, Methuku and Osthus. They proved the conjecture for every sufficiently large n. The arXiv record is dated 12 January 2021, and it appeared in Annals of Mathematics 198(2) in 2023. The threshold n₀ is not explicit in the sources I read. That result predates the window, and I found no event after 26 January 2024 that settles the conjecture for all n or for any further specific n. The post-window items are: two Bretto–Faisant–Hennecart arXiv papers (March 2024; the second published in Comptes Rendus 2025) on the stronger Berge–Füredi bound, which would imply EFL but is proved only under antirank or max-degree hypotheses and which the abstract does not claim gives EFL; Murff and Arsiwalla (October 2025), a conditional framework for Berge–Füredi that does not mention EFL; Kayll’s 2025 Mathematics Magazine exposition, which claims no new result; a Erdős Problems forum discussion (September–December 2025) and the site’s last edit (7 March 2026), which label the problem ‘decidable’ rather than solved; and a Google DeepMind Formal Conjectures Lean file (2026) whose large-n and n < 10 variants are labelled ‘research solved’ but use sorry. Where the close calls are: whether the site’s ‘decidable’ label or the repository’s ‘research solved’ label counts as settling the problem (both are in the record; the judging pass should decide); whether the Erdős–Füredi argument on Theorem 1.2 of arXiv:2110.06181 bears on EFL (it concerns k ≠ n, so I treat it as an analogue); and whether Hindman’s bound covers n = 10 (Wikipedia and erdosproblems disagree). The small-n picture is: Hindman (1981) verifies n ≤ 10 or n < 10; Romero and Alonso-Pecina (2014, record only) claim n ≤ 12; Kirchweger, Peitl and Szeider (SAT 2023) extend small cases by computer without stating ranges in the abstract. So the residue between the small-n verifications and the unstated n₀ is, on every source I read, uncovered, and the site calls it finite. For AI: none of the sources names an AI system for any EFL event. The KKKMO acknowledgements name only funders. The Erdős AI-contributions wiki (Tao’s GitHub page, last updated 30 June 2026, read through a summarising fetch) does not list #19. The Formal Conjectures file has no AI references. The AI-related Erdős results I found, including the May 2026 unit-distance disproof, the Aletheia study, and the Erdős #728 and #1026 work, all concern other problems. The 2015 claims by Lee and by Hegde and Dara are not AI-related, and their status is unresolved by any source I read. Two statements are unverified: the Frontiers of Science award to the KKKMO authors in 2024, which appeared only in search snippets, and the Discrete Mathematics 2021 publication of Alesandroni, which came from a citing listing.
competing_reading: Read as settled: the 2021 proof was refereed and published in the Annals. Lovász called it ‘essentially proved’. The Erdős site’s own forum leans to ‘more solved than open’ (Tao’s thread, Bloom’s comment that a bias towards ‘for all large enough integers’ is good enough), and the repository labels the large-n variant ‘research solved’. The remaining range is finite and checkable, and the question is about all n, so the bullet is answered in substance by a 2021 event that predates the window. Read as not settled: the bullet asks about every n. The theorem gives sufficiently large n with no explicit n₀. No source I read gives a finite check covering the gap between the small-n verifications and n₀. The site itself declines the solved label and calls the problem ‘decidable’, and the Lean proofs of the main and large-n statements are sorry-based.
what_would_settle_it: An explicit n₀ in KKKMO or in a later paper, together with a published computation covering all n below it (the SAT 2023 extension ranges, or a newer exhaustive check). A next status review of erdosproblems.com #19 would also settle the site’s label. The primary text of Hindman (1981) would settle n < 10 versus n ≤ 10. A completed Lean proof of the large-n theorem, free of sorry, would settle the formal status.

judgement.why: The statement is the conjecture for every n. KKKMO (2021, Annals 2023) proves it for all sufficiently large n with an unstated threshold, so it is a refereed, digested case and not the whole: a finite range of n remains, and erdosproblems itself calls the problem only 'decidable'. It predates the snapshot. The 2015 claims of a full proof (Lee; Hegde–Dara) are set aside as not credible. Each has several F10 signals: no uptake in a decade on a landmark problem, later papers by top researchers still calling the conjecture open, and in Hegde–Dara's case the authors' own later partial results. Hindman, Romero–Alonso-Pecina and the SAT 2023 work are finite checks (instances). Kahn's (1+o(1))n, Horák–Tuza and Hegde–Dara 2018 are bounds. The codegree t≥2 result, the fractional version, Mubayi–Verstraete and the Berge–Füredi results under extra hypotheses are variants. The post-snapshot items are none or variants: the conditional Berge–Füredi papers, an exposition, a forum label discussion, and a sorry-based Lean file. No event credits any AI system.
judgement.doubts: The KKKMO threshold n₀ is not stated anywhere in the record, so the size of the finite residue is unknown. BFH-a's actual theorems were not read; a snippet says a result on antirank ≥ √n may bear on EFL, and I scored it none on the abstract. BFH-b could arguably be a case of EFL if its hypotheses include linear hypergraphs with a bounded max degree; the record does not establish that. I scored it variant.
